episodes.214501: A backdoor front pushed through northeast and east-central NM and ended up along the east slopes of the central mountain chain come midday July 31st. Higher moisture behind the front, and lift along the front resulted in thunderstorm development across the central mountain chain during the early afternoon. Storms congealed into a line as they moved east and southeast across the eastern highlands and plains resulting in severe thunderstorm wind gusts near Cuero in Guadalupe County, Tucumcari and Clayton Municipal Airports, and a mesonet station in far northeast Lincoln County. The line also resulted in thunderstorm wind damage at a CoCoRaHS observer's residence south of Fort Sumner. The line of thunderstorms moved southeast into west Texas during the mid to late evening hours while the backdoor front pushed through the gaps of the central mountain chain resulting in gusty east canyon winds across the Santa Fe and Albuquerque Metros.
episodes.214519: During the afternoon and evening of August 1st, 2026, a modestly unstable and moisture-rich air mass interacted with a low pressure system moving across central Indiana. High precipitable water values and slow storm motion generated an environment favorable for torrential rainfall. Meanwhile, the modestly unstable airmass along with an enhancement of wind shear from the approaching system supported isolated severe thunderstorms.||The severe episode began at 16:20 EST in Marion County, where a brief EF-0 tornado with estimated peak winds of 76 mph touched down. The path length was 0.22 miles and the path width was 100 yards. The tornado uprooted and snapped multiple trees, caused minor siding damage to structures, and displaced a truck trailer into a parked vehicle. As the convection progressed eastward into Shelby, Henry, and Rush counties through 17:10 EST, straight-line thunderstorm wind gusts reached up to 70 mph (61 knots). These winds snapped and uprooted numerous trees, broke a home window, and flipped a metal shed.||Simultaneously, high rainfall rates of one to three inches per hour led to flash flooding in Marion and Shelby County as storm totals reached between 2.00 to 5.19 inches. In Marion County, heavy runoff forced the closure of the Interstate 465 and Interstate 70 exit ramp. In Shelby County, torrential downpours caused flooding on Interstate 74. Vehicles were also forced to turn around near Locust Street in Shelbyville due to high water.
episodes.214535: Slow moving thunderstorms over portions of Irwin, Ben Hill, and Berrien counties resulted in flash flooding during the first few days of August.
episodes.214542: A waterspout was sighted by Brunswick County EM.
episodes.214544: Higher surface moisture was in place across central and eastern NM on August 1st behind a backdoor front with upper level high pressure over Arizona and Utah. Daytime heating resulted in the development of thunderstorms across the higher terrain midday. One storm became severe near Mora and produced half dollar to ping pong ball size hail in town as well as flash flooding damage on Highway 94 from Mora, NM to the Mora and San Miguel County line. Storms moved south and southeast and coalesced into a broken line across the highlands of central New Mexico and the eastern plains during the afternoon and early evening hours resulting in severe thunderstorm wind gusts at several sites across White Sands Missile Range and localized flash flooding near Capitan. Storms tapered off across southern New Mexico during the late evening hours.
episodes.214556: Two rounds of thunderstorms impacted Middle Tennessee of August 1, 2026. The first round developed early in the morning and produced heavy rain, especially for urban areas around the Nashville metro area which caused a couple of flooding reports. The second round developed through the afternoon and evening hours as a front tracked through Middle Tennessee. These thunderstorms became more robust as they moved onto the Cumberland Plateau with two weak tornadoes produced in Cumberland and Fentress counties.

episodes.214643: A cold front moving through Central Alabama during the evening of August 1 sparked several line segments of mostly sub-severe thunderstorms. One cluster of storms in Talladega County produced a couple instances of tree damage.
episodes.214687: A heavy thunderstorm remained stationary and dumped over 6 inches of rain in rural sections of Williamsburg, SC.
episodes.214718: A decaying cluster of storms moved into northern portions of the area during the late evening/overnight hours of the 31st. These storms had produced a strong outflow boundary, which moved across the area and produced severe wind gusts in several locations. Strong to severe gusts persisted for over an hour in some locations after the boundary moved through and storms had decayed.

episodes.214742: An isolated thunderstorm produced very localized gale-force winds just offshore of Annapolis, Maryland.
episodes.214747: By the middle of the afternoon of the 31st, a cold front stalled out across the extreme southern Texas Panhandle. Strong surface heating ahead of the front allowed storms to develop along the leading edge of the front creating severe wind gusts in Childress County. A second round of storms came during the evening hours from the west. Thunderstorms initially developed off of the higher terrain of eastern New Mexico into the Raton Mesa. As these storms progressed southeastward they eventually grew upscale along numerous outflow boundaries spreading into the South Plains. A dry sub-cloud layer allowed these storms to become outflow dominant creating numerous severe wind gusts through the late evening hours.
episodes.214762: Scattered convection developed within an weak to moderately unstable environment during the afternoon on 8/1. Strong west to east moisture advection occurred with PWATs rising from around 1.5-1.7 inches in the morning to around 2.3-2.5 inches by early evening. A stalled frontal boundary provided a focus for low level convergence and nearly parallel mid level flow to the boundary orientation allowed  for training storms resulting in urban flash flooding.

episodes.214946: Scattered slow moving thunderstorms produced some minor road flooding in Dale county.
episodes.216136: An upper level low slowly tracked across central Illinois on August 1st, resulting in bands of showers and thunderstorms.  The heaviest rain focused over Vermilion County, where up to 4 inches of rain was measured and flash flooding occurred.  Several funnel clouds were reported east of I-55 as well.
episodes.216199: A few isolated severe thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts on the evening of July 31 across portions of south central Missouri. There were a few reports of trees downed or damaged across Texas and Shannon counties.
episodes.216286: A storm system moved across the area during the late afternoon and evening hours on the 31st and brought scattered storms to the area during the afternoon and evening. These storms produced several clouds.  One of these storms produced a tornado near the Cedar Rapids Eastern Iowa Airport. This tornado was rated EFU because there was no visible damage.
episodes.216380: Moist west-southwesterly flow ahead of an approaching cold front triggered showers and storms to move east-northeasterly up from the northeastern Gulf into the Suwannee Valley and into inland southeast Georgia in the afternoon hours.
episodes.216403: Periods of heavy rain along with scattered thunderstorms moved across parts of northeast Illinois from early morning through the evening of August 1st which caused localized flooding.
episodes.216530: Multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms produced several wind gusts in excess of 34 knots.
episodes.216869: A tropical wave moving across the region produced scattered showers and thunderstorms on the 1st of August. A waterspout was sighted over the Atlantic coastal waters of Puerto Rico, just north of San Juan.
episodes.217010: Slow moving thunderstorms dumped heavy rainfall across Bay county and resulted in flash flooding.  In addition, scattered afternoon and evening thunderstorms produced sporadic wind damage across the area.
episodes.217044: An upper high was located over southern New Mexico with some modest mid-level moisture present.  The location of the upper high kept thunderstorm motion very slow and over an inch and a half of rain was reported in the area.
episodes.217045: An upper high over southern New Mexico but with modest mid level moisture and high temperatures over 105 degrees helped produce gusty thunderstorms over El Paso with wind gusts up to 64 mph.
episodes.217207: During the afternoon a broken line of severe thunderstorms moved southeast through central and southeast Missouri. On its track, a few cells produced 3 tornadoes as well as tree and structural damage.
episodes.217663: A warm and moist airmass residing within a warm-sector well ahead of an approaching trough along with modest southerly winds along the coast led to showers across coastal waters capable of producing waterspouts shifting onshore.
episodes.217664: A warm and moist airmass residing within a warm-sector well ahead of an approaching trough along with modest southerly winds along the coast led to showers across coastal waters capable of producing waterspouts shifting onshore.
episodes.217843: A mid-level trough containing a nearly closed 500 mb low gradually moved across the Ohio Valley during the day on August 1st. An occluding surface low with a narrow warm sector was associated with the mid-level disturbance, and this narrow warm sector extended from north to south across central Kentucky during the afternoon and evening hours. Within the warm sector, roughly 1500 to 2000 J/kg of MLCAPE was present as dewpoint temperatures near the surface rose into the low-to-mid 70s. Effective shear was fairly strong for early August, with around 30-35 knots present on mesoanalysis. Showers and thunderstorms developed along the cold front into a broken line, with most of the line of storms remaining sub-severe. However, one storm was able to produce isolated wind damage to a shed and a tree in Warren County, with no other severe weather observed on this day.
episodes.217897: Southeast low level flow brought in good low level moisture to the Borderland with increasing northerly flow aloft.  An upper level disturbance triggered thunderstorms over the Sacramento Mountains which moved quickly south through eastern El Paso County and brought damaging winds to Socorro.
episodes.217898: Southeast low level flow brought in good low level moisture to southern New Mexico with increasing northerly flow aloft. An upper level disturbance triggered thunderstorms over the higher terrain with training storms resulting in flash flooding in Otero and Grant counties.  A dust storm and large hail were also reported in southwest New Mexico.
episodes.218085: Scattered thunderstorms moved across portions of west central Indiana during the afternoon and evening of August 1st producing heavy rain and localized flooding.
episodes.218108: A cluster of strong thunderstorms moved southward along the Middle Texas Coast during the early morning hours on August 2nd. Strong downbursts brought winds of 39 to 44 mph along the bays, islands, and nearshore water of the Middle Texas Coast.
episodes.218205: Moderately strong instability coupled with weak shear produced isolated strong to severe thunderstorms in primarily southeastern Tennessee. A weak tornado was produced by a supercell thunderstorm in far northern Bledsoe County. This is the 8th recorded tornado to occur in the month of August in NWS Morristown's database. Additionally, heavy rainfall from storms later in the evening led to significant flash flooding near the towns of Ducktown and Copperhill.

events.narrative: A well-defined waterspout reported by a trained spotter and observed on Surfline webcams developed from a shower offshore of Folly Beach, SC, just north of the Folly Beach Pier at 123 PM. The waterspout moved slowly west-northwest over the ocean for about 10 minutes before moving onshore as a tornado at 233 PM,  just south of the 3rd Street East public beach access point at latitude 32.6562 and longitude -79.9357.

The National Weather Service confirmed an EF0 tornado with an estimated maximum wind speed of 55 mph in Charleston County occurring from 133 PM to 134 PM. ||A well-defined waterspout reported by a trained spotter and observed on Surfline webcams developed from a shower offshore of Folly Beach, SC, just north of the Folly Beach Pier, before moving slowly west-northwest onshore as a tornado at 133 PM,  just south of the 3rd Street East public beach access point. The tornado moved across the beach, throwing a number of a tents, chairs and beach coverings into the air before dissipating along East Arctic Avenue at 134 PM. Damage was minimal, with only minor impacts noted to low-growth beach vegetation and no damage to nearby trees or homes. Despite the tornado moving directly through a large group of people, no injuries have been reported.

The tornado initially began in Dearborn County at 1732EST. Damage was first observed just east of Lawrenceville, along Batta Road, near the Batta and Legion Road intersection. Some roof damage to farm buildings was observed and a large farm wagon was overturned. The tornado appeared to cross over farm fields where crops were flattened. The tornado then crossed Legion Road where several large trees were damaged or snapped. Peak wind in this area was estimated to be near 70 mph.||The tornado continued north-northeast and produced tree damage as well as garage door damage along Trackville Road, just north of Old Hickory Road. Peak wind in this area was estimated to be between 70 and 75 mph.||At 1737EST, the tornado moved into Franklin County, about 1.5 miles west-northwest of St Leon.  It continued north-northeast across southern Franklin County before it dissipated at 1743EST, about 2 miles southwest of Cedar Grove.

The tornado began at 1732EST in Dearborn County, about 1 mile east-southeast of Lawrenceville. From there, it moved north-northeast and entered Franklin County at 1737EST, about 1.5 miles west-northwest of St Leon. As the tornado continued north-northeast across Franklin County, it produced roof damage to a single family home as well as roof and wall damage to barns just north of County Line Road. Peak winds in this area were estimated to be between 75 and 80 mph.||The tornado continued north-northeast and affected properties just northwest of the intersection of Saint Peters and Stone Roads, where roof damage occurred to a single family home and three barns were destroyed. In addition, some pine trees were snapped and hard trees were damaged.  Based on the damage, winds in this area were estimated to be 90 mph.||The tornado continued to move north-northeast along a narrow path through southeast Franklin County and produced additional barn and tree damage along Wewe Hill Road. This damage was consistent with winds between 70 and 75 mph.||The tornado is believed to have then dissipated at 1743EST, just north of where Wewe Hill Road becomes west to east, about 2 miles southwest of Cedar Grove.
KVIA reported downed power poles and other storm damage near Socorro.

Multiple videos and photos showed several inches of standing water flooding multiple roads and yards across Otterbein. A video showed a few inches of flowing water across the intersection of County Line Road and W 600 N County Road. A personal weather station measured 5.68 inches of rain in Otterbein in 3 hours ending at 19:00 EST.
Call center reported numerous reports of water over the roads at 630 PM.
County EM shared photos of washed out roads at low water crossings along Arena Rd and McCauley Rd.
Photos and videos showed several inches of flowing water across River Road just south of Route 30. Most yards were flooded in the vicinity. Possible flooding from Hickory Creek.

The start of the tornado occurred in  Bledsoe County near Grapevine Road about one quarter of mile south of the Cumberland County line. Several trees were uprooted. No  structures were affected in Bledsoe County.  This tornado continued onwards into Cumberland County just west of Old Grape Vine Road. Maximum wind speed was 75 mph.

An EF-0 tornado touched down near Grapevine Road in Bledsoe County and moved northeast into Cumberland County. The tornado uprooted trees, removed shingles, and damaged multiple outdoor buildings and a barn. The tornado continued to track to the northeast, crossing a wooded area before lifting near Jerry Edmonds Road. Damages are a rough estimate.
Shaw Air Force Base measured 4.11 inches of rain as of 7:27pm, fell over the last 80 minutes.

A brief EF-0 tornado touched down near Heinss Road in Fentress County. The tornado snapped treetops and uprooted a few trees. It continued to track to the northeast before lifting near Baseline Road. Damages are a rough estimate.
Several trees and limbs were downed along Shade Tree Rd near Alpine.
Trees were downed and blocking Cedars Road near Munford.
A tree was downed onto the roadway in the 1700 block of U.S. Route 42 East.
Video showed Governors Highway flooded near Governors Trail Park with at least one car stalled. Several inches of standing water was reported on Scott Drive near Thornwood Drive.
A tree fell onto Elliston-Napoleon Road.

The first known damage occurred in the 1600-1700 block of Surface Road. There was some minor roof damage to well-built homes. One barn was destroyed, with cinder block wall collapse, and some sheet metal roofing material was thrown into the field to the east.||Damage was then observed in the 1300-1400 block of Surface Road, where significant roof damage was noted at two homes, with sections of roofing material entirely removed. This damage supported wind speed estimates of 100 mph. Other homes in the area had some minor roof damage. Tree damage was also extensive in the back yards of these homes, with several large healthy trees snapped.||Drone images also depicted significant corn field damage in the vicinity of Surface Road. This damage also extended well to the east of Surface Road. Some of this corn field damage was from the tornado, but there was also a large expanse of flattened corn to the north of the path of the tornado, especially northeast of the bend on Surface Road. Much of the northern extent of the corn damage was oriented from northeast to southwest, suggesting a wide swath of strong inflow in the opposite direction of the motion of the tornado. No damage of any kind was observed closer to State Route 726.
